newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil investment banks face fierce competition.
newsitem.headline: Brazil investment banks face fierce competition.

text.p: Brazilian investment bankers admit they will work up a sweat this year beating back stiff competition, particularly from foreign banks, but they still see room for growth.
"Competition is getting stronger but with the economy growing four or five percent a year, there will be room for everyone," said Luiz Fernando Fleury, executive director at Rio-based Banco Marka.

Investment banking in Brazil has grown rapidly in recent years as the country's economic opening created a huge demand for underwriting of debt and stock issues and advising on corporate restructurings, mergers and acquisitions.
Brazil's 31-month-old stabilization drive has allowed local companies to gamble on economic growth and seek financing for expansion locally and abroad with the advice of investment banks.
The result has been a boom for local investment banks, whose profits soared last year.

Banco Marka, for instance, saw net profit rise 144.6 percent in 1996 over the prior year due mostly to its management of over $1.2 billion in debt, including Eurobond, commercial paper and securitization deals, in domestic and global markets.
The bank expects continued sharp growth in coming years.
"We are sure that underwriting and securitization deals will explode," said Marka's Fleury.

Over the past several years, the promise of Brazil's investment banking sector also has led foreign banks to open offices or expand operations in the country, intensifying not only the battle for clients but also for talented market professionals.
"They began to seek the best Brazilian traders, analysts and executives," said a local banker, who asked not to be named.

Moreover, competition among banks to lead manage a high number of new deals has been so strong that Eurobond launch prices have dropped sharply since last year, reducing spreads and tightening profit margins, traders said.

As a result of low inflation and other macroeconomic changes, asset management has become an attractive market niche for domestic and foreign investment banks. But competition also has become stiffer, bankers said.
"The money will move to the banks that offer the most sophisticated products with the highest return," said Claudio Coutinho, executive director at Banco da Bahia investment bank.
Currently, the bank manages $600 million in local and foreign investment, a portfolio which the bank plans to double in the next two years, he said.
Banco da Bahia's 1996 earnings are estimated at $73 million, up 52 percent from the previous year, mostly as a result of corporate and commercial brokerage activities.
